comments.author: amluto
comments.text:
> Depth-wise cross-attention (split Q/K/V): While standard transformer attention operates across tokens in a sequence, DCA applies attention across layers in depth. Each token queries a dynamically weighted mix of all prior layer embeddings, unlocking the model's full historical context without the computational penalty usually required to scale traditional attention.
I’ve often thought that something like this might lead to a real solution to the infamous strawberry problem.
Ignoring pesky issues like tokenization, the actual input data is visible to the model as the embedding fed to the first layer, but the first layer is probably nowhere near smart enough to understand that the model is trying to count R instances.  But by the time whatever layer is reached that might understand the goal, the non-wasteful part of the low-level memory (the K’s and V’s from the first layer) can’t be queried any more.
But this cross-depth attention can query them!
Admittedly, there are holes in this argument.  Beyond just tokenization (to the extent that the model can see letters at all, it is reconstructing them), the attention mechanism doesn’t really have a clean “count the hits” operation.

Generally goes unnoticed (though not unmentioned), but until after the Xantia, the suspension system also included the brakes and the steering (which would technically not be permitted under modern EU car standards); which meant a leak would eventually not just cause a loss of suspension, but also a loss of steering and braking.
Why incorporate the braking and the suspension?  The mechanical height regulator could "feel" how much fluid it needed to fill the suspension with, in order to obtain the desired ride height; which meant it "knew" how heavy the vehicle was loaded, and thus apply the brakes accordingly.  This is why in a proper Citroën hydraulic car, the brake pedal feels "weird", in that it doesn't go far down (and quickly becomes hard to press) (the DS tried to make this less confusion by making the pedal a "mushroom" button instead); because the idea is that you should apply gentle braking, and the car will figure out the necessary amount of braking force required (unlike just hitting the pedal like in a normal car, which would result in an almost hard stop).
Why the steering then?  I think that's more of a convenience thing, mechanically speaking, as it was already there

comments.author: glimshe
comments.text:
For every dollar gained by will-put-you-in-jail
long-term
automatic copyrights, we probably lose tens, if not hundreds, of dollars of potential economic value. Very few people care about most protected works, and the vast majority enter a limbo and stay there, unused and forever forgotten. I doubt original authors would want that as the fate of their labor.
A simple solution exists: mandate renewal and increasing fees after a certain number of years. Make 10 year protections automatic and free, then start charging small fees with a registration requirement, increasing the fees every 5 years. It isn't unreasonable to ask for, let's say, US$ 10K to protect a 50-year old work.
Most developed economies are deep in debt and this would be a very progressive tax, ultimately only charging "people" (aka mega corporations) who benefit economically from the work.
